title: Comfort of the afflicted

segments.voice: Yesterday, tower of ivory and house of gold: pictures borrowed from a love song and a golden Temple. Your line was poetry for a mother. Did you find a picture for someone you love? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-three.

A hospital corridor, late at night. Someone has just had bad news, and a friend sits down next to them. The friend doesn't explain anything. Doesn't fix anything. Fetches a coffee, sits back down, and stays. Weeks later, the one who got the news may not recall a single sentence from that night, only that someone stayed. Further down the Litany of Loreto, after the towers and the gold, the titles change their tone. Health of the sick. Refuge of sinners. Comforter of the afflicted. Help of Christians. The poetry comes down to the ground, to hospital corridors and bad nights. Today's word is the one in the middle.
screen: `A FRIEND WHO STAYS.` → `HEALTH OF THE SICK, REFUGE OF SINNERS.` → `COMFORT OF THE AFFLICTED.`

segments.voice: In the litany's Latin, the title is consolatrix afflictorum: the one who consoles the afflicted, the people weighed down. Catholics give Mary this name, and the reason begins with her own grief. When she brings her baby to the Temple, an old man named Simeon takes him in his arms and then turns to her. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." The comforter in this title is not someone who was spared. Then the cross. John's Gospel names who was there, and it starts with her: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother." Look at what the text gives her to do. No speech. No miracle. She stood. Some Catholics find in that one verb a whole way of comforting: you don't leave, even when there's nothing to say. Then Saint Paul adds a third turn. Writing to the church in Corinth, he says that God comforts us in all our trouble so that we can comfort others in theirs, with the same comfort we were given. Comfort, for Paul, travels. It is received and then handed on. That is how Catholics hear this title. Mary, who knew the sword and stood at the cross, passes on the comfort she received, and when they pray comforter of the afflicted, pray for us, they bring her the people who are going under. And the title quietly describes a job. Anyone can take a shift: the friend in the corridor, the neighbor with a casserole, the text that says I'm here and asks nothing back.
screen: `SHE KNEW THE SWORD HERSELF.` · `AT THE CROSS, SHE STOOD.` · `COMFORT RECEIVED, THEN HANDED ON.` · `A JOB ANYONE CAN TAKE A SHIFT IN.` · then, large: `NOW THERE STOOD BY THE CROSS OF JESUS, HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who is carrying something heavy right now. An illness, a loss, a job gone, a worry they keep mentioning. Stay with them in your mind for a few breaths, the way the friend stays in the corridor. Don't plan advice. Then choose one small act of comfort for today: a short message that asks nothing, a call, a visit, a meal left at the door. If you pray, you can name them and add the litany's line, comforter of the afflicted, pray for us. If you don't, simply hold them, and keep your plan. The bell holds the time.
Comfort of the afflicted. In Latin, consolatrix afflictorum: a title of Mary, who knew the sword and stood at the cross, for everyone who is weighed down. Today's word.
Your line: comfort of the afflicted. Today, do the one small act you chose, and when you're with them, say less and stay longer. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics call on Mary as Comforter of the Afflicted in the Litany of Loreto, and parishes and hospital chaplains often bring the title to people who are sick or grieving, alongside visits and practical help.

trapdoor: what you thought: comfort means making the pain go away.
what it means: a title of Mary, who knew grief herself and stood at the cross. comfort as staying, then handing it on.

what a scholar hears: consolatrix afflictorum, set among the litany's titles of mercy, with Simeon's sword (Luke 2:35), the cross (John 19:25) and Paul's comfort passed on (2 Corinthians 1:4) behind it.
